newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Britain outlines private finance scheme to Morocco.
newsitem.headline: Britain outlines private finance scheme to Morocco.

text.p: A British specialist started to brief Moroccan officials and business leaders on Tuesday about how London has harnessed private finance to provide services in contracts totalling $10 billion.
Mike Williams, treasury director of industry policy, told reporters at a news briefing that Private Finance Initiative (PFI) was a new way for government to finance services they needed.

"The government buys the services, and the private sector provides them," he said. The concept was based on the idea governments were interested in buying "a flow of services and not an asset," he said.
"It's a different way of procuring services," he told Reuters. "And it ensures value for money because you leave the private sector with the choice of the way of doing it."

He said "the concept started crystalising about five years ago, and we started about three years ago. About 7 billion (pounds), or about $10 billion, is involved in agreed contracts...for PFI so far."
Three billion pounds ($4.9 billion) of this total was for the Channel tunnel train operating between Britain and France.
In addition to providing incentive, PFI allows governments to spread spending over the life of a project instead of all "upfront." PFI also moves risk to the private sector from the state.
This has made drawing up contracts more complex. Contracts are usually long-term, up to 25 or even 40 years, said Williams.
Using prisons as an example, he said "the state doesn't want the prison buildings but what they provide (and) the availability of the services that go with them, with provision of secure places."
Privatisation Minister Abderrahman Saadi invited Williams to Morocco after a meeting earlier this year at the Treasury in London, Williams said.

Under contracts signed by the British government, he said, the private sector was also providing roads, rail services, bridges, underground trains, non-clinical services in the health sector and information technology services.

PFI gave private industry incentives to avoid the pitfalls the state faced when it carried out projects and when overruns on time and cost became common. By paying only when services were provided, private industry was focused on completing contracts rapidly.

Nine major road schemes in Britain produced under PFI schemes had produced 15 percent in savings, Williams said. Prison buildings under PFI deals saved the government 10 percent and halved the time involved, he said.
But Williams warned PFI was not suitable for all countries, particularly those with weak governments and where private investors could not be sure of continued payment over the contract period.

Youssef Fehry Fassy, technical counsellor at the Moroccan privatisation ministry, said other countries looking at PFI included Argentine, Chile, Uruguay, Paraguay, Malaysia and South Africa. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
